figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Effect of patch size (nano backbone; five-fold, mean$\pm$std). (a) Per-patch (Stage-1) accuracy and image-level accuracy under majority voting and AMIL: all rise with patch size and the image-level curves plateau near $512$ px, well above the per-patch accuracy that aggregation is built from. (b) The AMIL$-$voting gap (left axis) shrinks as patch size grows, while the effective fraction of patches attended (right axis) rises toward one, so at large patches the attention distribution is near-uniform and pooling behaves like voting. (H1), (H2), (H6)
figures.headline: Per-patch and image-level accuracy both rise with patch size, while the attention-over-voting gap shrinks as attention becomes near-uniform.
citing_sentences: Per-patch (Stage-1) accuracy increases monotonically with patch size, from $75.6\%$ at $160$ px to $89.6\%$ at $512$ px (Figure 1), confirming H1: larger patches, which capture more of the trunk’s bark structure, are individually more discriminative.

The advantage of learned aggregation over majority voting is small at every patch size and declines monotonically as patch size increases, from $+0.73$ pp at $160$ px to $+0.16$ pp at $512$ px (Figure 1).

It rises with patch size and plateaus near $512$ px ($94.7\%$ at $384$ to $94.9\%$ at $512$; Figure 1), whereas the whole-image case, which admits no aggregation because its bag contains a single instance, falls well below it ($91.9\%$).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Image-level accuracy as a function of the number of patches available at inference (nano backbone, $224$ px; mean$\pm$std over five folds). Both aggregation rules improve steeply up to about $16$–$32$ patches and plateau thereafter, so a few dozen patches per trunk suffice; AMIL stays above majority voting throughout, by a margin that is largest when patches are scarce and narrows as the bag grows. (H7)
figures.headline: Image-level accuracy saturates after about 16–32 patches, and attention pooling stays above voting at every bag size.
citing_sentences: Image-level accuracy increases with the number of patches available at inference and saturates well before the full bag is used (Figure 2).

Each patch is shaded by its attention weight relative to the uniform weight $1/N$ (colour bar, $0.25\times$ to $4\times$); brighter patches receive more weight. The attention is largely diffuse: most patches receive near-uniform weight and the few higher-weight patches show no consistent spatial structure.
figures.headline: Attention over the trunk is largely diffuse, with most patches receiving near-uniform weight and no consistent spatial structure.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows the learned attention over representative trunks of four species, expressed relative to the uniform weight $1/N$.

Rows are true species, columns predicted; species are ordered by genus, so that the predominantly intra-genus confusions appear as near-diagonal blocks.
figures.headline: Errors for the recommended configuration fall mostly within genera, forming near-diagonal blocks for congeneric species.
citing_sentences: For the recommended configuration (nano backbone, $512$ px, AMIL), the image-level confusion matrix is shown in Figure 4; per-class precision, recall, and $F_{1}$ are reported in Table A4.
Nonetheless, the errors are concentrated exactly where congeneric bark is most alike, as the near-diagonal, within-genus structure of Figure 4 makes plain.

abstract: Background: The automatic identification of tree species from bark photographs is of practical interest for forestry inventory and for the wood-processing industry, yet the numerous design choices that govern the accuracy of deep-learning approaches have not been studied systematically, and some prior results may be inflated by the leakage of images of the same trunk across training and test partitions. Methods: A systematic ablation study is conducted on the public BarkNet 1.0 dataset (20 species) under the established tree-level, leakage-safe partitioning scheme. Using ConvNeXt-V2 backbones, the following factors are varied in turn and evaluated by five-fold cross-validation: the patch size at which bark is sampled (five sizes), the strategy by which per-patch predictions are aggregated into an image-level decision, the training regime (single- versus two-stage), the backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and the number of patches available at inference. Results: Per-patch accuracy rises monotonically with patch size (from $75.6\%$ at $160$ px to $89.6\%$ at $512$ px), and image-level accuracy rises in step, plateauing near $94.9\%$ around $512$ px. Learned aggregation exceeds majority voting by at most $0.7$ pp, an advantage that shrinks as patches grow and the attention distribution becomes near-uniform. Backbone capacity (pico to tiny) alters accuracy by less than a point, and two-stage training does not offer an advantage over one-stage training. Whole-image classification ($91.9\%$) trails patch-based aggregation despite its larger field of view, since it admits no bag to average over; and accuracy increases with the number of patches available at inference, saturating around $64$ patches. Conclusions: The study yields a simple recommended configuration: patches as large as possible while still leaving enough patches to average over (around $512$ px here), with a nano backbone. It also quantifies the second-order role of learned aggregation and model capacity, providing a reproducible reference point for practitioners and future research.

sections.body: The paper motivates bark-based species identification for forestry and wood processing. It notes that prior systems mostly used leaves or flowers, while bark is visible year-round. The authors state that design choices such as patch resolution, aggregation rule, training procedure, backbone capacity and patch count have been studied in isolation rather than jointly. They also note that image-level splits on trunks with several photographs can leak near-identical views into test sets and inflate accuracy. The study therefore runs a systematic ablation under the tree-level split of Carpentier et al. and does not introduce a new architecture.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Bark identification is practical, but design choices for tile-based deep learning have not been compared jointly, and image-level splits can leak.

sections.body: The study uses the 20 retained species of BarkNet 1.0, comprising 998 trees and 23,271 images, split at the tree level with five-fold cross-validation. Each photograph is tiled into square patches at five sizes from 160 to 512 px. Patch predictions are aggregated by majority voting, attention-based multiple instance learning, a fixed-head vote, or a whole-image classifier. Backbones are ConvNeXt-V2 pico, nano and tiny. Hyperparameters were tuned once for the nano backbone at 224 px and transferred to other settings. Eight hypotheses (H1 to H8) isolate each design choice. Reported metrics are top-1 image-level accuracy and macro-averaged F1.
sections.heading: Materials and Methods
sections.headline: Tree-level five-fold tests on BarkNet 1.0 vary patch size, aggregation, training, backbone capacity and bag size, with eight hypotheses.

sections.body: Per-patch accuracy rises monotonically from 75.6% at 160 px to 89.6% at 512 px. Image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% at 512 px, while the whole-image baseline reaches 91.9%. Attention pooling exceeds majority voting by +0.73 pp at 160 px, falling to +0.16 pp at 512 px, as the effective fraction of patches attended rises to 99.0%. Two-stage training gives 91.5% against 92.8% for single-stage, so it offers no advantage. Backbone capacity changes accuracy by under a point, and accuracy saturates near 64 test-time patches. The attention maps show no interpretable pattern. The authors note the whole-image baseline is downsampled to 224 px, which partly explains its lower score.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% at 512 px, and learned aggregation beats voting by at most 0.73 pp.

sections.body: The discussion condenses the ablations into a recommended setup. Patch size is the dominant factor and should be as large as the image allows while keeping enough patches to aggregate; the optimum on BarkNet 1.0 is around 512 px. The nano backbone gives the best accuracy-to-size trade-off. Single-stage training is sufficient. Attention pooling is consistently at least as accurate as voting for a negligible parameter increase. The section compares results with Carpentier et al., where tree-level attention pooling reaches 97.8% against their 97.81%. Stated limitations include a single dataset, class imbalance, hyperparameters tuned only for nano at 224 px, and no image-level significance tests.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Recommended setup is patches around 512 px with a nano backbone; aggregation and training matter less.

sections.body: The conclusions restate the main findings for bark-based species classification under tree-level evaluation on BarkNet 1.0. Patch size is identified as the principal factor, with an optimum reached around 512 px, beyond which too few patches remain. Backbone capacity and training regime are described as second-order, with ConvNeXt-V2 nano giving the best trade-off. Learned attention pooling is described as at least as accurate as majority voting for a negligible parameter cost. The authors note that about a dozen patches per trunk approach full accuracy. They suggest the findings may inform other tile-based fine-grained recognition pipelines.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: Patch size dominates accuracy, so the study recommends the largest patches that still leave enough to average over, with a nano backbone.
